title: Goal Setting
coreMove: Pair specific targets with stretch and reality checks so the metric steers the mission without replacing it.
sourcePressure: The chapter uses SMART goals, stretch goals, and the Yom Kippur War to show that targets shape action, ambition, and strategic judgment, sometimes helpfully and sometimes dangerously.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Treating any clear metric or any big ambition as automatically good.

sourceAnchors.name: SMART goals
sourceAnchors.detail: the sidecar supports SMART goals as a chapter anchor for usable concrete targets
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: SMART goals should feel like a handle, not a shrine: they make the next move visible but cannot decide what matters by themselves.

sourceAnchors.name: stretch goals
sourceAnchors.detail: the sidecar supports stretch goals as the ambition counterweight to concrete specificity
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: A stretch goal earns its place only when it pulls new behavior out of the room instead of becoming theater.

sourceAnchors.name: Yom Kippur War
sourceAnchors.detail: the subtitle directly supports the Yom Kippur War as the cautionary historical anchor but not detailed chronology
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The Yom Kippur War belongs here as a warning that planning frames can sharpen judgment or blind it.

hook: Person at a meeting realizes the real lesson
The day starts with a dashboard
counterintuition: Productivity is not doing more faster
The problem is not effort but something deeper

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person direct address, retrospective, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.domain: a community health clinic trying to reduce missed diabetes follow-ups
exampleSpecs.audience: a clinic director revising a vague improvement aim
exampleSpecs.stakes: patients keep falling through the cracks while the team celebrates activity counts
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Rachel rewrites the goal from more outreach to a dated follow-up target, then adds a mission check: patients seen, not calls logged
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A stack of callback sheets sits beside an untouched glucose meter box

exampleSpecs.domain: an amateur orchestra preparing for a regional competition
exampleSpecs.audience: a conductor deciding whether to chase a perfect tempo score
exampleSpecs.stakes: musicians may hit the metronome and lose the piece's emotional lift
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Luca keeps the tempo target but adds a listening test after rehearsal so the measurable goal serves the musical aim
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "We can play it clean and still make it dead," the first violin says

exampleSpecs.domain: a warehouse safety team after a quarter with too many near misses
exampleSpecs.audience: a safety lead under pressure to produce a bold turnaround goal
exampleSpecs.stakes: a dramatic zero-incident poster could drive underreporting
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: It took Camille two underreported near misses to see that the stretch goal needed a paired reporting target
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Camille two quiet Fridays to realize the zero-incident poster had worked too well

exampleSpecs.domain: a high-school debate squad choosing goals for nationals
exampleSpecs.audience: a coach balancing ambition with weekly practice design
exampleSpecs.stakes: students may choose a trophy dream with no practice path
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Daniel turns the trophy aim into specific drills while keeping one stretch practice that forces new argument styles
exampleSpecs.firstImage: How does a goal get big enough to pull effort without floating away from Tuesday practice?
mustAvoid: letting the question hook replace the visible action beat

exampleSpecs.domain: a climate nonprofit setting donor targets before a legislative season
exampleSpecs.audience: a campaign manager caught between fundraising numbers and policy change
exampleSpecs.stakes: the team could hit the donation goal while missing the vote window
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: At 4:05 p.m., Kasia ties the donor target to one legislative milestone so the metric cannot outrank the mission
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 4:05 p.m., the donor thermometer graphic is already full and the vote count is not

exampleSpecs.domain: a small craft brewery deciding whether to double production
exampleSpecs.audience: a founder using growth targets without losing quality control
exampleSpecs.stakes: a stretch production goal could overload fermentation capacity and ruin a release
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Tomas asks the team to predict what will break first under doubled output, then adjusts the target around the bottleneck instead of the vanity number
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The new fermenter smells faintly of steel and citrus sanitizer

skillTargets: diagnose when a SMART target has become narrow scorekeeping
add stretch without losing operational grip
evaluate goals by whether they preserve contact with the mission

tryThisNowSpec: Take one current goal and add the missing half: if it is vague, define the next measurable step; if it is narrow, write the larger mission it must not betray.
